tutorialHtml:
DENIZ AKKABAK · VIKING AGE TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MADE IN INVIDEO · invideo.io/i/DENIZ-ig

Valhalla Delivery

The Viking Age, filmed as if somebody had been standing there with a phone. Fifteen deadpan anachronism gags, bookended by one parcel, built end to end inside invideo with Nano Banana Pro stills and Seedance 2.5 video.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

PIPELINE NANO BANANA PRO → SEEDANCE 2.5 · FORMAT 16:9 · 15 SCENES · 1:16 · BUILT IN INVIDEO

Every scene in this film runs on one rule: put exactly one modern object into the Viking Age, let it cause one real, physical consequence, and make sure nobody in the frame thinks anything strange is happening. The comedy is never the object itself. It is the deadpan. A Viking with a parcel scanner is mildly funny; a Viking scanning a box as it flies out of a siege catapult, with the bored focus of a courier on his fortieth drop of the day, filmed by someone who just happened to be standing there, is the clip people send to their friends.

That second half, the someone-was-there feeling, is the real craft. The stills are written as unedited phone footage with real-world imperfection baked in, and the videos are directed as a bystander’s shaky, late-reacting phone clip, never a film crew. Below is the full workflow, every still, and every prompt exactly as it was run inside invideo.

THE PIPELINE AT A GLANCE

  1. 01

    Still — Nano Banana Pro

    One 16:9, 2K still per gag, generated inside invideo. The prompt describes the gag, then a fixed realism block; a separate negative-prompt field blocks the cinematic look and any camera interface.

  2. 02

    Video — Seedance 2.5

    The still goes in as @Image 1, the exact first frame. 10 seconds, 1080p, audio off. Each prompt is a timecoded mini-sketch with a payoff in the last beats, shot by an imaginary bystander’s phone.

  3. 03

    Edit — invideo timeline

    Each 10-second take is trimmed to its best four to six seconds, cut on the beat of the music, and the moments where the model slipped are left on the cutting-room floor.

STEP 01 — THE FORMULA

One Object, One Consequence, Nobody Reacts

Pick objects everyone recognises instantly and that have a famous, specific behaviour: an outboard motor refuses to start, a card terminal prints an endless receipt, a key fob makes the lights blink, a defibrillator brings someone back. Then pick a piece of the Viking world that already carries a story, such as Danegeld, berserkers, Valkyries, Odin’s ravens or runestones. The best gags explain a piece of history or myth with a modern routine.

Write the consequence into the video prompt as the final beat, and give it to a character with a straight face: the chieftain locking his ship without looking back, the Valkyrie sighing as her warrior wakes up, the crew rowing past a motor that finally starts. If a character laughs, the joke dies.

STEP 02 — SETTING UP IN INVIDEO

Two Models, One Workspace

  1. 01

    Nano Banana Pro

    Aspect ratio 16:9, resolution 2K. Paste the image prompt into the prompt field and the negative list into the separate negative-prompt field.

  2. 02

    Seedance 2.5 (reference to video)

    Attach the finished still as the only reference image so it becomes @Image 1. Duration 10 seconds, resolution 1080p, audio generation off: the music goes on in the edit.

  3. 03

    Timeline

    Drop all clips on one invideo timeline, add the track, and trim each take to the window where the gag reads cleanly.

STEP 03 — THE REALISM BLOCK

Make It Look Like Nobody Planned It

Nano Banana Pro is the reason the stills read as real: it defaults to flat, deep-focus, slightly messy phone-like images instead of the glossy, dramatic light other models reach for. The realism block pushes it further: deep depth of field, crunchy sharpening, white balance a little off, people cut off by the frame edges, someone half blocking the view, dirt and mismatched clothing.

Two traps worth knowing. Describe the image as phone footage too literally and the model draws a phone camera interface on top: REC dots, timestamps, viewfinder brackets. These prompts describe “the natural look of everyday smartphone footage”, add “Clean full-frame image with no interface or overlays of any kind”, and list every overlay in the negative field; when a date stamp still slipped into the Odin still, the regenerated prompt named it explicitly. Second, Vikings did not wear horned helmets, and image models love them, so “iron helmets without horns” sits in the realism block and “horned helmets” sits in every negative list. Brand names also stay out: the flat-pack leaflet and the hair styler are described by shape and colour, never by brand, so no fake logo appears.

SCENE 01 — NANO BANANA PRO → SEEDANCE 2.5

Next-Day Delivery

The film opens on the joke the whole title is built on: a siege catapult used as a courier. The Viking holding a modern parcel scanner up at the flying box, like a driver logging a drop-off, is the detail that makes it read as a routine shift rather than a stunt.

STEP 04

Anatomy — Why These Prompts Work

  1. 01

    The contract

    “FORMAT: 16:9, one continuous 10 second take, no cuts, real-time speed.” One take with no cuts keeps Seedance from inventing an edit, and real-time speed stops it drifting into slow motion, which instantly reads as cinematic instead of caught-on-camera.

  2. 02

    The first-frame lock

    “@Image 1 is the EXACT FIRST FRAME. Start on it with no change.” The still carries all the realism work, so the video must inherit it untouched: same faces, same props, same light, same texture.

  3. 03

    Timecoded beats

    Every prompt is a four-beat sketch with timestamps (0-3s, 3-5s, 5-7s, 7-10s): setup, escalation, the accident, the deadpan reaction. Seedance follows the order, and the edit can grab the payoff knowing where it lands.

  4. 04

    The bystander camera

    “Filmed on a smartphone held by an ordinary bystander … reacting a beat late.” Hand shake, jerky digital zooms, focus hunting and exposure pumping are what turn a generated clip into something that feels witnessed.

  5. 05

    The deadpan rule

    “Deadpan … Nobody looks at the camera.” The characters never acknowledge the absurdity and never perform for the lens. That restraint is the comedy.

  6. 06

    The operator’s hands

    “No fingers, hands or phone of the operator ever visible in frame.” Ask for a phone camera and Seedance may draw the phone-holder’s hand. Naming it in the camera block and the negative prompt shuts it out.

  7. 07

    The insurance

    Two negative lists work together: the image negative field bans the cinematic grade, bokeh, plastic skin and every camera overlay, and the video NEGATIVE PROMPT bans gimbal moves, morphing, extra limbs and people appearing from nowhere.

THE RESULT

Output — Valhalla Delivery

Check your own cut against three things. Does every scene have a physical consequence, not just a funny object? Does every character stay deadpan? And does the camera feel like somebody who was there by accident and pulled their phone out a second too late? If all three hold, the delivery lands.

ONE OBJECT · ONE CONSEQUENCE · NOBODY REACTS

Valhalla was never a place. It was a delivery address.

Swap the Vikings for Rome, Egypt or the Middle Ages, swap the catapult for whatever modern object has a famous behaviour, and the skeleton carries any era: a realism block that makes the still look found, a timecoded four-beat sketch with the accident at the end, and a bystander’s phone that reacts a beat late.
